vsm1.1:143.0: (vi) The Defiling and the Cleansing of Virtue
vsm1.1:143.1: However, it was also asked (vi) WHAT IS THE DEFILING OF IT? and WHAT IS THE CLEANSING OF IT?
vsm1.1:143.2: We answer that virtue’s tornness, etc., is its defiling, and that its untornness, etc., is its cleansing.
vsm1.1:143.3:
Now, that tornness, etc., are comprised under the breach that has gain, fame, etc.,
as its cause, and under the seven bonds of sexuality.
vsm1.1:143.4: When a man has broken the training course at the beginning or at the end in any instance of the seven classes of offences,
vsm1.1:143.5: his virtue is called torn, like a cloth that is cut at the edge.
vsm1.1:143.6: But when he has broken it in the middle, it is called rent, like a cloth that is rent in the middle.
vsm1.1:143.7: When he has broken it twice or thrice in succession,
vsm1.1:143.8:
it is called blotched, like a cow whose body is some such colour as black or red with a discrepant
colour appearing on the back or the belly.
vsm1.1:143.9: When he has broken it all over at intervals,
vsm1.1:143.10: it is called mottled, like a cow speckled all over with discrepant-coloured spots at intervals.
vsm1.1:143.11: This in the first place, is how there comes to be tornness with the breach that has gain, etc., as its cause.
vsm1.1:144.1: And likewise with the seven bonds of sexuality; for this is said by the Blessed One:
vsm1.1:144.2:
“Here, brahman, some ascetic or brahman claims to lead the life of purity rightly; for he does
not enter into actual sexual intercourse with women. Yet he agrees to massage, manipulation,
bathing and rubbing down by women. He enjoys it, desires it and takes satisfaction in it.
vsm1.1:144.3: This is what is torn, rent, blotched and mottled in one who leads the life of purity.
vsm1.1:144.4:
This man is said to lead a life of purity that is unclean. As one who is bound by the bond of sexuality,
he will not be released from birth, ageing and death …
vsm1.1:144.5: he will not be released from suffering, I say.
vsm1.1:145.1: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to these things, yet he jokes, plays and amuses himself with women …
vsm1.1:146.1: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to these things, yet he gazes and stares at women eye to eye …
vsm1.1:147.1:
“Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to these things, yet he listens to the sound of women
through a wall or through a fence as they laugh or talk or sing or weep …
vsm1.1:148.1:
“Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to these things, yet he recalls
laughs and talks and games that he formerly had with women …
vsm1.1:149.1:
“Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to these things, yet he sees a householder or a householder’s
son possessed of, endowed with, and indulging in, the five cords of sense desire …
vsm1.1:150.1:
“Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to these things, yet he leads the life of purity aspiring to some order of deities,
thinking ‘Through this rite (virtue) or this ritual (vow) or this asceticism I shall become a great deity or some lesser deity.’
vsm1.1:150.2: He enjoys it, desires it, and takes satisfaction in it.
vsm1.1:150.3:
This, brahman, is what is torn, rent, blotched and mottled in one who leads the life of purity.
This man … will not be released from suffering, I say” (A IV 54–56).
vsm1.1:150.4:
This is how tornness, etc., should be understood as included under the breach that has gain,
etc., as its cause and under the seven bonds of sexuality.
vsm1.1:151.1:
Untornness, however, is accomplished by the complete non-breaking of the training
precepts, by making amends for those broken for which amends should be made,
vsm1.1:151.2:
by the absence of the seven bonds of sexuality, and, as well, by the non-arising of such evil
things as anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obduracy, presumption,
pride (conceit), haughtiness, conceit (vanity), and negligence (MN 7),
vsm1.1:151.3: and by the arising of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement (MN 24).
vsm1.1:152.1: Virtues not broken for the purpose of gain, etc.,
vsm1.1:152.2: and rectified by making amends after being broken by the faults of negligence, etc.,
vsm1.1:152.3:
and not damaged by the bonds of sexuality and by such evil things as anger and enmity,
are called entirely untorn, unrent, unblotched, and unmottled.
vsm1.1:152.4:
And those same virtues are liberating since they bring about the state of a freeman, and praised by the wise
since it is by the wise that they are praised,
vsm1.1:152.5:
and unadhered-to since they are not adhered to by means of craving and views, and conducive to concentration
since they conduce to access concentration or to absorption concentration.
vsm1.1:152.6: That is why their untornness, etc., should be understood as “cleansing” (see also VII.101f.).
vsm1.1:153.1: This cleansing comes about in two ways: through seeing the danger of failure in virtue,
vsm1.1:153.2: and through seeing the benefit of perfected virtue.
vsm1.1:153.3:
Herein, the danger of failure in virtue can be seen in accordance with such suttas as that beginning,
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for the unvirtuous in the failure of virtue” (A III 252).
vsm1.1:154.1:
Furthermore, on account of his unvirtuousness an unvirtuous person is displeasing to deities and human
beings, is uninstructable by his fellows in the life of purity,
vsm1.1:154.2:
suffers when unvirtuousness is censured, and is remorseful when the virtuous are praised.
Owing to that unvirtuousness he is as ugly as hemp cloth.
vsm1.1:154.3: Contact with him is painful because those who fall in with his views are brought to long-lasting suffering in the states of loss.
vsm1.1:154.4: He is worthless because he causes no great fruit to accrue to those who give him gifts.
vsm1.1:154.5: He is as hard to purify as a cesspit many years old.
vsm1.1:154.6: He is like a log from a pyre (see It 99); for he is outside both recluseship and the lay state.
vsm1.1:154.7: Though claiming the bhikkhu state he is no bhikkhu, so he is like a donkey following a herd of cattle.
vsm1.1:154.8: He is always nervous, like a man who is everyone’s enemy.
vsm1.1:154.9: He is as unfit to live with as a dead carcase.
vsm1.1:154.10:
Though he may have the qualities of learning, etc., he is as unfit for the homage of his fellows
in the life of purity as a charnel-ground fire is for that of brahmans.
vsm1.1:154.11: He is as incapable of reaching the distinction of attainment as a blind man is of seeing a visible object.
vsm1.1:154.12: He is as careless of the Good Law as a guttersnipe is of a kingdom.
vsm1.1:154.13: Though he fancies he is happy, yet he suffers because he reaps suffering as told in the Discourse on the Mass of Fire (A IV 128–34).
vsm1.1:155.1:
Now, the Blessed One has shown that when the unvirtuous have their minds captured by pleasure and satisfaction
in the indulgence of the five cords of sense desires, in receiving salutation, in being honoured, etc.,
the result of that kamma, directly visible in all ways, is very violent pain, with that kamma as its condition,
capable of producing a gush of hot blood by causing agony of heart with the mere recollection of it. Here is the text:
vsm1.1:155.2: “Bhikkhus, do you see that great mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing?— Yes, venerable sir.—
vsm1.1:155.3:
What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one gone forth should sit down or lie down embracing
that mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing, or that he should sit down or lie down embracing a warrior-noble
maiden or a brahman maiden or a maiden of householder family, with soft, delicate hands and feet?—
vsm1.1:155.4: It would be better, venerable sir, that he should sit down or lie down embracing a warrior-noble maiden …
vsm1.1:155.5: It would be painful, venerable sir, if he sat down or lay down embracing that great mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing.
vsm1.1:156.1:
“I say to you, bhikkhus, I declare to you, bhikkhus, that it would be better for one gone forth who is unvirtuous,
who is evil-natured, of unclean and suspect habits, secretive of his acts, who is not an ascetic and claims to be one, who
does not lead the life of purity and claims to do so, who is rotten within, lecherous, and full of corruption, to sit
down or lie down embracing that great mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing.
vsm1.1:156.2:
Why is that? By his doing so, bhikkhus, he might come to death or deadly suffering, yet he would
not on that account, on the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in states of loss, in an unhappy
destiny, in perdition, in hell. But if one who is unvirtuous, evil-natured … and full of corruption, should sit down or lie
down embracing a warrior-noble maiden … that would be long for his harm and suffering: on the break-up of the body,
after death, he would reappear in states of loss, in an unhappy destiny, in perdition, in hell” (A IV 128–29).
vsm1.1:157.1:
Having thus shown by means of the analogy of the mass of fire the suffering that is bound up with women and has as its condition
the indulgence of the five cords of sense desires by the unvirtuous, to the same intent he showed, by the following
similes of the horse-hair rope, the sharp spear, the iron sheet, the iron ball, the iron bed,
the iron chair, and the iron cauldron, the pain that has as its condition acceptance of homage and reverential
salutation, and the use of robes, alms food, bed and chair, and dwelling by unvirtuous bhikkhus:
vsm1.1:157.2:
“What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong horse-hair rope twisted round both
legs by a strong man and tightened so that it cut through the outer skin, and having cut through the outer skin
it cut through the inner skin, and having cut through the inner skin it cut through the flesh,
vsm1.1:157.3:
and having cut through the flesh it cut through the sinews, and having cut through the sinews it cut
through the bones, and having cut through the bones it remained crushing the bone marrow—
vsm1.1:157.4: or that he should consent to the homage of great warrior-nobles, great brahmans, great householders?” (A IV 129).
vsm1.1:157.5:
And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong
man wound one’s breast with a sharp spear tempered in oil—
vsm1.1:157.6: or that he should consent to the reverential salutation of great warrior-nobles, great brahmans, great householders?” (A IV 130).
vsm1.1:157.7:
And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one’s body should be wrapped by a strong
man in a red-hot iron sheet burning, blazing and glowing—
vsm1.1:157.8: or that he should use robes given out of faith by great warrior-nobles, great brahmans, great householders?” (A IV 130–31).
vsm1.1:157.9:
And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one’s mouth should be prised open by a strong man with red-hot iron
tongs burning, blazing and glowing, and that into his mouth should be put a red-hot iron ball burning, blazing and glowing,
vsm1.1:157.10:
which burns his lips and burns his mouth and tongue and throat and belly and passes
out below carrying with it his bowels and entrails—
vsm1.1:157.11: or that he should use alms food given out of faith by great warrior-nobles …?” (A IV 131–32).
vsm1.1:157.12:
And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong man seize him by the head or seize
him by the shoulders and seat him or lay him on a red-hot iron bed or iron chair, burning, blazing and glowing—
vsm1.1:157.13: or that he should use a bed or chair given out of faith by great warrior-nobles … ?” (A IV 132–33).
vsm1.1:157.14:
And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong man take him feet up and head
down and plunge him into a red-hot metal cauldron burning, blazing and glowing, to be boiled there in a swirl of froth,
vsm1.1:157.15:
and as he boils in the swirl of froth to be swept now up, now down, and now across—or that he should
use a dwelling given out of faith by great warrior-nobles … ?” (A IV 133–34).
vsm1.1:157.16:
Thus, by these similes of the horse-hair rope, the sharp spear, the iron sheet, the iron ball,
the iron bed and chair, and the iron cauldron, he showed the pain that has as its condition the use of homage,
reverential salutation, robes, alms food, bed and chair, and dwelling.
vsm1.1:158.1:
What pleasure has a man of broken virtue
Forsaking not sense pleasures, which bear fruit
Of pain more violent even than the pain
In the embracing of a mass of fire?
vsm1.1:158.2:
What pleasure has he in accepting homage
Who, having failed in virtue, must partake
Of pain that will excel in agony
The crushing of his legs with horse-hair ropes?
vsm1.1:158.3:
What pleasure has a man devoid of virtue
Accepting salutations of the faithful,
Which is the cause of pain acuter still
Than pain produced by stabbing with a spear?
vsm1.1:158.4:
What is the pleasure in the use of garments
For one without restraint, whereby in hell
He will for long be forced to undergo
The contact of the blazing iron sheet?
vsm1.1:158.5:
Although to him his alms food may seem tasty,
Who has no virtue, it is direst poison,
Because of which he surely will be made
For long to swallow burning iron balls.
vsm1.1:158.6:
And when the virtueless make use of couches
And chairs, though reckoned pleasing, it is pain
Because they will be tortured long indeed
On red-hot blazing iron beds and chairs.
vsm1.1:158.7:
Then what delight is there for one unvirtuous
Inhabiting a dwelling given in faith,
Since for that reason he will have to dwell
Shut up inside a blazing iron pan?
vsm1.1:158.8:
The Teacher of the world, in him condemning,
Described him in these terms: “Of suspect habits,
Full of corruption, lecherous as well,
By nature evil, rotten too within.”
vsm1.1:158.9:
So out upon the life of him abiding
Without restraint, of him that wears the guise
Of the ascetic that he will not be,
And damages and undermines himself!
vsm1.1:158.10:
What is the life he leads, since any person,
No matter who, with virtue to his credit
Avoids it here, as those that would look well
Keep far away from dung or from a corpse?
vsm1.1:158.11:
He is not free from any sort of terror,
Though free enough from pleasure of attainment;
While heaven’s door is bolted fast against him,
He is well set upon the road to hell.
vsm1.1:158.12:
Who else if not one destitute of virtue
More fit to be the object of compassion?
Many indeed and grave are the defects
That brand a man neglectful of his virtue.
vsm1.1:158.13:
Seeing danger in the failure of virtue should be understood as reviewing in such ways as these. And seeing
benefits in perfected virtue should be understood in the opposite sense. Furthermore:
vsm1.1:159.1:
His virtue is immaculate,
His wearing of the bowl and robes
Gives pleasure and inspires trust,
His going forth will bear its fruit.
vsm1.1:159.2:
A bhikkhu in his virtue pure
Has never fear that self-reproach
Will enter in his heart: indeed
There is no darkness in the sun.
vsm1.1:159.3:
A bhikkhu in his virtue bright
Shines forth in the Ascetics’ Wood
As by the brightness of his beams
The moon lights up the firmament.
vsm1.1:159.4:
Now, if the bodily perfume
Of virtuous bhikkhus can succeed
In pleasing even deities,
What of the perfume of his virtue?
vsm1.1:159.5:
It is more perfect far than all
The other perfumes in the world,
Because the perfume virtue gives
Is borne unchecked in all directions.
vsm1.1:159.6:
The deeds done for a virtuous man,
Though they be few, will bear much fruit,
And so the virtuous man becomes
A vessel of honour and renown.
vsm1.1:159.7:
There are no cankers here and now
To plague the virtuous man at all;
The virtuous man digs out the root
Of suffering in lives to come.
vsm1.1:159.8:
Perfection among human kind
And even among deities.
If wished for, is not hard to gain
For him whose virtue is perfected;
vsm1.1:159.9:
But once his virtue is perfected,
His mind then seeks no other kind
han the perfection of Nibbāna,
The state where utter peace prevails.
vsm1.1:159.10:
Such is the blessed fruit of virtue,
Showing full many a varied form,
So let a wise man know it well
This root of all perfection’s branches.
vsm1.1:160.1: The mind of one who understands thus, shudders at failure in virtue and reaches out towards the perfecting of virtue.
vsm1.1:160.2:
So virtue should be cleansed with all care, seeing this danger of failure in virtue and this
benefit of the perfection of virtue in the way stated.
vsm1.1:161.1:
And at this point in the Path of Purification, which is shown under the headings of virtue, concentration and understanding
by the stanza, “When a wise man, established well in virtue” (§1), virtue, firstly, has been fully illustrated.
vsm1.1:161.2: The first chapter called “The Description of Virtue” in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.
